main_sections.title: Vitamin-M
main_sections.prose_summary: Vitamin-M is a gently comic yet deeply humane short story by Asha Nehemiah about the tensions and tenderness that arise when an elderly grandparent moves into a city flat. The narrative opens with Ravi's mother wishing someone would invent 'Vitamin-M' — a pill to improve old people's memories — unaware that her 75-year-old father, Grandpa, can hear her from his rocking chair. Grandpa has come to live with the family after a series of alarming incidents at his beloved small-town home: an accidental double dose of medicines led to hospitalisation, and a fall while pottering in his garden left him lying outside all night. Ravi's mother, Vidya, has locked up the house and brought him to their 'poky little flat' in the city against his wishes. Grandpa resents the loss of independence — he had managed house, cooking, and shopping alone for ten years after his wife's death — and bristles at being treated like a child. The central episode unfolds on the first day of Ravi's school holidays. After his mother leaves for work and instructs Ravi to keep Grandpa at home, Grandpa craftily manoeuvres a confession from Ravi that he has received no such instruction, then strides out with his mahogany walking stick (brass handle carved as an eagle's head) and yellow cap. Ravi is caught in a dilemma — he cannot accompany Grandpa openly without hurting his dignity, nor can he let him roam unsupervised. He follows Grandpa secretly, a comedy of errors ensuing: crouching behind an elephant-shaped bush in the children's park earns him the wrath of a mother and a crawl through the park on all fours; hiding behind a banyan tree at a tea stall provokes loud vendor women who mistake him for a new hawker; ducking into a shop next to the barber's lands him in a Ladies' Hairdressing Salon from which he is evicted amid shrieks. Grandpa, meanwhile, enjoys a sugary tea, two bananas, and an ice cream — all banned at home — and gives his yellow cap to a bald stranger at the barber shop as a generous gesture. Ravi, fooled by the stranger's cap and white clothes, boards a bus chasing the wrong man, and by the time he returns home, Grandpa is already safely asleep. The story concludes with a twist of wit: Grandpa coolly tells Ravi's mother that he had 'a quiet morning' but that Ravi had disappeared, embarrassing Ravi completely. Grandpa then reveals birthday gifts for everyone, correcting Ravi's mother when she assumes he has forgotten Ravi's birthday — it is Grandpa's own birthday, and he always gives gifts on that day. He suggests that Ravi's mother needs Vitamin-M herself, and presents Ravi with The Best Detective Stories, winking at his amateur surveillance. The story explores themes of intergenerational dignity and respect, the invisibility and infantilisation of the elderly, selective memory (Grandpa's chess knowledge is encyclopaedic though he forgets names), the tension between safety and autonomy, and the quiet love between grandparent and grandchild. The embedded story 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand (pp.120-125) appears as a *Learning Beyond the Text* supplementary reading and is not a separate main section.

listening.transcript_text: Dear students, welcome to today's session on meditation. Meditation is an important yogic practice commonly used for relaxation and stress management. Basically, meditation provides rest and peace to the mind. During meditation, all kinds of thoughts which cause stress are removed, resulting in an enhanced state of well-being, both physically and emotionally. After meditation, the person feels fresh and gains a new perspective on stressful situations. Meditation also helps to reduce negative emotions and increases self-awareness. I encourage you to start practising meditation on a regular basis and make it your routine — it will contribute to your overall well-being and positively influence your memory power. In fact, practising meditation regularly can help lessen exam-related pressure, allowing you to manage challenges with ease. So, let us begin the journey of meditation together.

main_sections.title: I Cannot Remember My Mother
main_sections.poem_text:
I cannot remember my mother
only sometimes in the midst of my play
a tune seems to hover over my playthings,
the tune of some song that she used to
hum while rocking my cradle.

I cannot remember my mother
but when in the early autumn morning
the smell of the shiuli flowers floats in the air
the scent of the morning service in the temple
comes to me as the scent of my mother.

I cannot remember my mother
only when from my bedroom window I send
my eyes into the blue of the distant sky,
I feel that the stillness of
my mother's gaze on my face
has spread all over the sky.
main_sections.poem_appreciation_summary: Rabindranath Tagore's three-stanza lyric traces the speaker's fragmented, sensory memory of a mother he lost too early to remember directly. Each stanza anchors a different sense: a hovering lullaby tune heard amid play (auditory); the scent of shiuli flowers in an autumn morning merging with the fragrance of temple worship (olfactory); the infinite stillness of the sky seen from a bedroom window that recalls the mother's gaze on the child's face (visual). The refrain 'I cannot remember my mother' — repeated as the opening of each stanza — paradoxically makes her presence pervasive. The poem's tone is tender and quietly melancholic, caught between loss and a deeper, instinctive belonging. Tagore employs imagery, symbolism (shiuli flowers as a symbol of the mother's gentle, devotional spirit; the sky as the eternal extension of her gaze), and refrain as its dominant devices.

listening.transcript_text: Four speakers share childhood memories. Speaker (i): As a child, when disheartened, the speaker's grandfather's advice about keeping morale high echoes in his mind. Grandfather would ask 'who is the bravest one?' and the speaker always shouted 'Me'. The voice and belief still uplift the speaker when feeling low. Speaker (ii): Childhood was about liberty — chasing butterflies, making paper boats in rain, playing on sandy beaches, returning home muddy to escape scolding. These carefree joys echo as simple, cherished memories. Speaker (iii): Cherished preparatory-school days include a grandma's sweet tolerance. Mornings meant sitting on grandpa's lap demanding comic-strip tales from newspapers, then pretending to retell stories in the kitchen and ending up babbling, forgetting the real narratives — beautiful memories that linger clearly. Speaker (iv): Childhood at the beach with parents is a cherished memory, until the family moved when the speaker was in Grade 1. Returning after a decade, the once serene beach is now crowded and the carefree days are replaced by a sense of distance within the family, highlighting a shift in generational connections.

Take turns to speak about it using the prompts given below: Introduce it briefly; Describe it in detail including sensory details; Narrate the specific memory associated with it; Explain how it has impacted your life; Summarise why this memory is meaningful to you even now. [Sentence starters provided: 'During my childhood…', 'Growing up, I fondly remember…', 'I have a clear memory of…', etc.]

I Imagine you had been on a school trip to a scenic place which appealed to all your senses. Write a diary entry describing the place and why it was a memorable experience. Contents: begin with day, date, and time; use only first person (I, my); capture sensory details; express emotions; focus on significant moments and experiences; conclude with reflection. [Note on diary format: Anne Frank and Zlata Filipovic began with 'Dear diary'; Samuel Pepys did not.]

I You read about the shiuli flowers from the poem. Gather more information on unique flowers of India — where they are found, how they look, what smell they emit, and what the historical significance is, if any. [Example given: Kurinji/Neelakurinji that blooms once in twelve years.] Add more flowers to this list. [Shiuli flowers info provided: known as Parijat/Parijata/Harsingar; revered for ceremonial purposes; release a sweet fragrance; associated with numerous Indian legends; bloom exclusively during the night.]

II You must have read poems and songs related to the theme of family, friends and their reminiscences, in English and also in your own language. Collect these poems and songs, and share with your classmates and teacher. Now, read and enjoy the poem given below. [Poem: 'I Remember, I Remember' by Thomas Hood — speaker remembers the house where they were born, the little window where the sun came peeping in at morn, roses red and white, violets and lily cups, lilacs where the robin built, and the laburnum set by a brother on his birthday, noting 'The tree is living yet!' — a nostalgic recollection of a childhood home and garden, contrasted with a wish that the night had taken the speaker's breath away, suggesting present-day melancholy.]
